newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Index-linked bonds beckon investors.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Index-linked bonds beckon investors.

text.p: Investors seeking to broaden their portfolios might consider index-linked bonds as the prospect of the launch of U.S. index-linked debt in early 1997 creates anomalies within the sector, analysts said on Friday.
Analysts said index-linked bonds from Canada, New Zealand and Australia may offer better returns than the speculated real yield from the U.S.
"Index-linked bonds are in a special situation at the moment," said Tim Knowles, director at Fleming Investment Management in London.
"The catalyst for it is the issuance of U.S. index-linked bonds next January, but what we don't know is at what price the U.S. is going to put it's index-linked bonds," he said.

Knowles said the thinking was that too high a real yield for index-linked bonds would damage the equities market, where yields on equities are low. But too low a real yield would leave other index-linked bonds more attractive.
The three countries to currently offer this opportunity were Canada, New Zealand and Australia, he said.

"If global inflation is not too much of a worry, you can make a case that if you are prepared to buy a U.S. index-linked bond, which may yield around three percent real, why shouldn't you buy a New Zealand index-linked bond?" said Knowles.
He said over the last few weeks, Canadian and New Zealand index-linked bonds had moved ahead strongly to catch up with the conventional bond markets in those countries.

Index-linked bonds, which offer a guaranteed return above the rate of inflation, can offer considerable benefits for issuing governments by reducing funding costs, increasing the range of debt instruments and acting as a useful tool to gauge inflation.

"In an environment where you have reasonably strong (economic) growth in the U.S. and the possiblity of a little pick-up in inflation next year, the idea of index-linked bonds seems very attractive," said Sonia Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London.
She said the idea was popular with retail buyers but could also be played to political and economic advantage by the U.S. government.

"Obviously the Treasury would have all the benefits of saving on interest costs and offering a broader range of debt instruments to investors, and also it's a good tool," she said. "The Bank of England is very fond of using it to monitor inflation expectations and the U.S. Treasury would enjoy having the same advanatage."

Britain has been issuing index-linked bonds since 1982. But some analysts say the merits of index-linked bonds as an inflationary tool are limited because of the illiquidity of the market in comparison with the conventional bond market.
"The relationship between the two doesn't move as much as inflation expectations might be expected to move," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.

He said fears of rising inflation in Britain had helped index-linked bonds recently and could continue to do so in the near future but the overall picture for inflation was positive, and longer term these fears were misplaced.

"We are still in a disinflationary global environment where inflation and official interest rates will remain low," said Lyons. "I'm still positive about conventional bonds but the market needs to be convinced that stronger growth does not mean higher inflation."
He said it had taken some time for the U.S. market to be convinced of this and might also take a little time to convince the British market.
Knowles agreed, "In many cases conventional bonds might do better than index-linked bonds," he said.
